988.title: Panja Sahib, 1922
988.hook: Sikhs lay on the railway to stop a train and feed the prisoners on it; two died
988.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the saka of Panja Sahib alongside the gurdwara's older story of Guru Nanak's handprint; pilgrims to Hasan Abdal touch the print in the stone, and the two men who died on the rails are honored as shaheeds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bagh, and your line was beaten, unbowed. Did a sharp word pass you without a sharper one coming back? Today, the prisoners from that garden are on a train. Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

Pots of dal and stacks of rotis, still warm, wrapped in cloth on a railway platform. The people who cooked them have heard that a train is coming through their town, carrying Sikh prisoners arrested at Guru ka Bagh, on their way to a distant jail. The cooks want to feed them. The station master says the train is not scheduled to stop here. So what do you do with a langar that has nowhere to go?
screen: `WARM FOOD ON A PLATFORM.` → `PRISONERS ON A TRAIN.` → `THE TRAIN WILL NOT STOP.`

segments.voice: First, the place. The town is Hasan Abdal, and its gurdwara is Panja Sahib. Sikh tradition tells that Guru Nanak rested there, and that a rock rolled down the hill toward him was stopped by his open hand, which left its print in the stone. Panja means the outstretched hand. Pilgrims still touch that print. Second, the track. When the request to stop was refused, members of the sangat went down onto the rails and lay across them, in the path of the train. Histories of the reform movement say the train ran over some of them before it came to a halt. Two men, Bhai Karam Singh and Bhai Partap Singh, died of their injuries. Third, the meal. The train had stopped. The food was handed through the windows, and the prisoners ate. That's today's line: they stopped the train. It wasn't done to block anyone or to win an argument. It was done so that hungry people could eat. Fourth, the root. At Ang 1245 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that the one who earns by honest work and gives some of it away with their own hand has recognized the way. The langar is that teaching made into a kitchen. At Panja Sahib, a town cooked for strangers, and then put their own bodies between the meal and the timetable. The place had long been remembered for one open hand. After that day it was remembered for many.
screen: `THE HANDPRINT IN THE STONE.` · `THE SANGAT LAY ON THE RAILS.` · `THE FOOD WENT THROUGH THE WINDOWS.` · `EARN, AND GIVE WITH YOUR HAND.` · then, large: `THEY STOPPED THE TRAIN.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with an open hand. Sit, and rest one hand on your knee, palm up, fingers spread, the way the panja is pictured. Breathe slowly. Bring to mind someone who might be hungry today: a neighbor, a coworker skipping lunch, a stranger you pass on the way home. Hold that person in mind as you breathe. Then think of one thing you could actually hand them: a meal, a snack, a grocery bag, a donation to a food bank. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Panja Sahib. The gurdwara of the handprint at Hasan Abdal, where the sangat lay on the rails to stop a train and feed the prisoners on it. Today's word.
Your line: they stopped the train. Today, feed someone in need: share a meal, buy a lunch, or give to a kitchen that feeds people. Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

989.title: Jaito, 1923
989.hook: a long peaceful campaign over the deposition of the ruler of Nabha
989.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Jaito morcha as one of the long peaceful campaigns of the gurdwara reform years; Gurdwara Gangsar at Jaito keeps its memory, and those killed on the way are honored as shaheeds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Panja Sahib, and your line was they stopped the train. Did you feed someone? Today, a campaign that didn't last an afternoon. It lasted a very long time. Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

A continuous reading of the Guru Granth Sahib is under way. Readers take turns, one after another, so the voice never stops, from the first page to the last. That unbroken reading is called an akhand path. Now the police walk into the gurdwara and the reader is taken away, mid-line. For the people sitting there, the question isn't politics anymore. A reading of the Guru has been cut off. What happens next will not be over in a day, or in a season.
screen: `AN UNBROKEN READING.` → `THE READER IS TAKEN AWAY.` → `A READING CUT OFF.`

segments.voice: First, the ruler. Maharaja Ripudaman Singh of Nabha, a small Sikh state, was known for his sympathy with the Akali reformers. The British government forced him to give up his throne. The Akalis took it as a blow aimed at the panth itself, and they gathered to protest. Second, the reading. At Gurdwara Gangsar in the town of Jaito, in Nabha, Sikhs held an akhand path for the deposed ruler. The authorities stopped it and arrested those present. Now the cause had a second side: the right to read the Guru Granth Sahib to the end. Third, the jathas. Group after group set out for Jaito to begin the reading again, and group after group was arrested. Histories of the movement record that one large jatha was fired on as it neared the town, and many were killed and wounded. Still the jathas kept coming, peacefully, month after month, until the reading was finally allowed to go on. That's today's line: long and peaceful. Fourth, the root. In the shaloks of Sheikh Farid kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, at Ang 1384, Farid says: make patience your bow, patience its string, and patience the arrow, and the Creator will not let you miss. Jaito asked for that kind of patience, not for a day but for seasons. The campaign wasn't one brave moment. It was the same quiet choice, made again each morning, by people who knew where the road led.
screen: `THE RULER OF NABHA DEPOSED.` · `THE AKHAND PATH CUT OFF.` · `JATHA AFTER JATHA, FOR MONTHS.` · `PATIENCE, THE BOW AND THE ARROW.` · then, large: `LONG AND PEACEFUL.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of steady return. Sit, and let your breath settle into a pace you could keep all day. Count each breath out, from one to ten, and then begin again at one. When your mind wanders, and it will, don't scold it. Just go back to one, the way a jatha set out again the next morning. Steady, not forced. If you pray, you can say Waheguru instead of the numbers, on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Jaito. The town in Nabha where an akhand path was cut off, and where jathas kept coming, peacefully, for months, until the reading could go on. Today's word.
Your line: long and peaceful. Today, pick one thing you've been tempted to give up on and take one more calm step on it, without forcing. Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

990.title: The Gurdwara Act, 1925
990.hook: the law passes historic gurdwaras to an elected Sikh body
990.howItsDone: Historic gurdwaras in Punjab are managed under the Sikh Gurdwaras Act by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, whose members are elected by Sikh voters; its elections and decisions are discussed and debated across the community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jaito, and your line was long and peaceful. Did you take one more calm step on something hard? Today, where all those long, peaceful marches led: to a law. Day nine hundred ninety.

A ballot paper, folded once, dropped into a box. It doesn't look like the end of a struggle. No march, no train on the rails, no police line. Just a voter, a list of names, and a choice. But in the story of the gurdwara reform movement, that small, dull act is the prize. For years, Sikhs had walked into beatings and arrests to answer one question: who should care for the Guru's houses? Today, the answer arrives in the plainest form there is. The Gurdwara Act.
screen: `A BALLOT IN A BOX.` → `NO MARCH, NO POLICE LINE.` → `THE ANSWER ARRIVES IN LAW.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Through the campaigns of the last weeks, at Nankana, bagh, Jaito and elsewhere, the reformers asked that historic gurdwaras be taken from hereditary mahants and returned to the sangat. Second, the law. The Sikh Gurdwaras Act was passed in Punjab. It named historic gurdwaras and placed their management under a Sikh body whose members were chosen by Sikh voters. That body soon took the name the reformers had already made famous: the SGPC. Third, what changed. Before, a shrine could pass from one mahant to his son or chosen disciple, like private property. After, those who ran it answered to an elected committee, and the committee answered to the sangat at the ballot box. That's today's line: peace won. The movement didn't take the gurdwaras by force. It kept walking until the law changed. Fourth, the root. At Ang 72 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak asks how the true sangat can be known, and answers: it is where the One Name alone is praised. The reformers' claim was that a gurdwara belongs to that sangat, not to a family. The Act wrote that claim into law. It didn't settle every argument. Sikhs have debated the elected body, its politics and its choices ever since, and they still do. But a debate held through votes and committees is itself part of what was won. A voter with a ballot paper is a strange kind of hero. At the end of this story, that's exactly who the hero is.
screen: `WHO CARES FOR THE GURU'S HOUSE?` · `A LAW FOR HISTORIC GURDWARAS.` · `ANSWERING TO THE SANGAT.` · `WHERE THE ONE NAME IS PRAISED.` · then, large: `PEACE WON.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for the things you share. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one place you hold in common with others: a gurdwara, a church, a school board, a library, a tenants' group, a town council. Something that isn't yours alone, and isn't anyone else's alone either. Breathe in, and picture the people who share it. Breathe out, and ask one quiet question: is there one way I could take part this month? If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Gurdwara, the door or house of the Guru: a law in Punjab placed historic gurdwaras under a Sikh body elected by Sikh voters, the fruit of peaceful campaigns. Today's word.
Your line: peace won. Today, vote or take part once: check your registration, attend a meeting, or volunteer for something you share with others. Day nine hundred ninety.

991.title: Master Tara Singh
991.hook: a schoolteacher who led the Akalis for decades
991.howItsDone: Master Tara Singh is remembered among Sikhs as a leader of the Akali Dal and the SGPC through the reform years and after; his life and decisions are discussed in Sikh histories, and his name is on schools and public places in Punjab.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurdwara, and your line was peace won. Did you take part in something shared? Today, one of the people who led the Akalis through those years and long after. Day nine hundred ninety-one.

Some nicknames outlive the job. A coach is still Coach at the grocery store years after the last game. A nurse is still the nurse at every family dinner. In Punjab, one Sikh leader kept a classroom title long after he'd left the classroom. Not General, not President, not Sardar. Master. As in schoolmaster. He led marches, negotiated with governments and went to jail, and people kept calling him the teacher. Today: Master Tara Singh.
screen: `A NICKNAME OUTLIVES THE JOB.` → `NOT GENERAL. NOT PRESIDENT.` → `MASTER, AS IN SCHOOLMASTER.`

segments.voice: First, the choice. Tara Singh was born into a Hindu family, and as a young man he chose the Sikh path and took amrit, the Khalsa initiation. That's how his biographers tell it, and it shaped him: he came to the panth by choice, and he defended it for the rest of his life. Second, the classroom. He studied at Khalsa College in Amritsar, which we met earlier in this block, and then became a teacher and a headmaster at a Khalsa school. Teaching, for him, wasn't a stop on the way to something else. It was how he understood leading: explain, persuade, keep the students together. Third, the Akalis. When the gurdwara reform movement rose, he joined it and soon stood among its leaders. He led the Akali Dal and the SGPC for many years, through the reform campaigns and later through the hard years around the partition of Punjab. He was jailed more than once. Sikhs still argue about his politics and his decisions, and historians weigh them differently. That's a real argument, and it isn't settled here. But friends and critics alike remember the name he kept. That's today's line: the teacher-leader. Fourth, the root. The Asa di Var opens, at Ang 462 of the Guru Granth Sahib, with Guru Nanak saying he is a sacrifice to his Guru a hundred times a day, the Guru who made angels out of humans without delay. In Gurbani that gratitude belongs to the Guru. But it colors the way Sikhs speak of anyone who teaches, and it helps explain why a classroom title could become a name of respect that lasted a lifetime.

segments.voice: Two minutes with a teacher. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one teacher who changed something in you. It might have been a schoolteacher, a coach, a grandparent, a boss, someone at the gurdwara who showed you how to sit with the Guru Granth Sahib. Picture their face, their voice, the way they explained things. Breathe in, and remember one thing they said that stayed. Breathe out, and let a little gratitude come with it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Tara Singh, a schoolteacher and headmaster who led the Akalis for decades, and was called by the teacher's title, Master, all his life. Today's word.

992.title: Writing the Rehat Maryada
992.hook: from the 1930s scholars and leaders drafted a shared code, published in 1950
992.howItsDone: Gurdwaras managed by the SGPC, and Sikh families who choose it, follow the Sikh Rehat Maryada published by the SGPC for daily prayers, services, the ardas and ceremonies; some Sikh groups keep their own rehat on certain points.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Master Tara Singh, and your line was the teacher-leader. Did you thank someone who taught you? Today, a different kind of work: not a march, but a document. Day nine hundred ninety-two.

Who does the dishes? When do the lights go out? Do phones come to the table? Writing down a family's house rules sounds simple until everyone has an opinion, and every opinion comes with a story about how Grandma did it. Now make the family a whole panth, spread across villages and cities and countries, with customs that grew up differently in different places. And try to write one short booklet that they can share. That's today.
screen: `WRITING DOWN THE HOUSE RULES.` → `EVERYONE HAS AN OPINION.` → `ONE BOOKLET FOR A WHOLE PANTH.`

segments.voice: First, the need. Once the gurdwaras were in the sangat's hands, a practical question followed: how should things be done inside them, and in a Sikh's own life? Practices varied from place to place. The reformers wanted a shared standard. Second, the drafting. Under the SGPC, scholars, granthis and leaders met over years, wrote drafts, sent them out for comment, argued and revised. It was slow work. A code that only a few people wrote would be a code only a few people kept. Third, the code. The Sikh Rehat Maryada opens by saying who a Sikh is: one who believes in the One Immortal Being, in the ten Gurus from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh, in the Guru Granth Sahib and the Gurus' teaching, and in the amrit given by the tenth Guru, and who holds to no other religion. Then it covers the daily prayers, how to sit before the Guru Granth Sahib, the ardas, the langar, the birth of a child, marriage and death, and the amrit ceremony. That's today's line: a code, agreed. Fourth, what agreed means. It doesn't mean every Sikh group signed every line. Some, like the Akhand Kirtani Jatha we'll meet tomorrow, the Damdami Taksal and Nihang groups, keep their own rehat on certain points. The SGPC's code guides the gurdwaras it manages, and others beyond them, and it sits alongside those others. What it gave the panth was a shared starting page: a place to point to and say, this is how we do it here.
screen: `HOW SHOULD THINGS BE DONE?` · `YEARS OF DRAFTS AND DEBATE.` · `WHO IS A SIKH, AND HOW TO LIVE.` · `A SHARED STARTING PAGE.` · then, large: `A CODE, AGREED.`

segments.voice: Two minutes toward your own short code. Sit, and let your breath slow. Ask yourself a simple question: what are three things I want to do, every day, no matter what? Not big promises. Small things: wake and sit quietly, speak honestly, share something. Let one come to mind, and hold it for a few breaths. Then a second. Then a third. Don't write yet; just notice which ones stay. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Rehat Maryada, the way of living and the accepted custom: the shared code of Sikh life and practice, drafted and debated under the SGPC over years. Today's word.
Your line: a code, agreed. Today, write your own simple code: three short lines on a card or in your phone, and read them once before bed. Day nine hundred ninety-two.

993.title: Bhai Randhir Singh
993.hook: a revolutionary and devotee whose followers founded the Akhand Kirtani Jatha
993.howItsDone: The Akhand Kirtani Jatha holds kirtan programs, including all-night kirtan, and its members keep a strict rehat; Bhai Randhir Singh's writings, including his prison letters, are read among his followers and others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, writing the Rehat Maryada, and your line was a code, agreed. Did you write your three lines? Today, a man who kept his own code inside a prison. Day nine hundred ninety-three.

A guard's footsteps go down a stone corridor at night, past an iron door, and fade. From behind the door comes a voice singing shabads from the Guru Granth Sahib, steady and unhurried, as if the room were a gurdwara. The guards have heard it before. They will hear it again tomorrow. The man singing has been sentenced for plotting against the British government, and he has many years still to serve. The singing does not stop. Today: Jail Letters.
screen: `FOOTSTEPS IN A STONE CORRIDOR.` → `A VOICE SINGING SHABADS.` → `THE SINGING DOES NOT STOP.`

segments.voice: First, the two sides of him. Bhai Randhir Singh came from the village of Narangwal in Punjab. He was drawn into the Ghadar plans against British rule that we met earlier in this block, and he was arrested and given a long prison sentence. He was a revolutionary. He was also, before and after, a man of deep devotion. Second, the rehat in jail. In jail he was expected to eat what he was given and live as the jail decided. He held to his own strict discipline as a Khalsa Sikh, including about the food he would accept, and when it was refused he went without, for long stretches. His own account of these years, his Jail Letters, describes the hunger, the punishments and the stubbornness in plain terms. Third, the singing. Through all of it he kept up kirtan, singing the Gurus' hymns, alone or with any Sikh prisoner who would join him. That's today's line: kirtan in prison. Fourth, the root and the fruit. At Ang 1075 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says that in this dark age, kirtan, singing the Lord's praise, is supreme. After his release, those who gathered around Bhai Randhir Singh formed the Akhand Kirtani Jatha, known for kirtan that can go on through the whole night, and for a strict rehat of their own. Some Sikhs follow that path closely; others admire it from a distance. Either way, it began in a cell, with one voice that wouldn't stop singing.
screen: `REVOLUTIONARY AND DEVOTEE.` · `HE KEPT HIS REHAT IN JAIL.` · `HE KEPT SINGING.` · `KIRTAN THROUGH THE NIGHT.` · then, large: `KIRTAN IN PRISON.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a song. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind something hard you're carrying right now: a worry, a loss, a situation you can't leave. Then let a song come to mind, one that steadies you. A shabad, a hymn, a lullaby, anything. You don't have to sing aloud. Hum it quietly, or hear it inside, line by line, while the hard thing sits beside you. Let the song keep its own pace. If you pray, you can let Waheguru be the song, on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Jail Letters, Bhai Randhir Singh's own account of the hunger, the punishments and the kirtan that carried him through long years in prison.
Your line: kirtan in prison. Today, sing through a hardship: when something heavy comes, hum one steady song, even under your breath. Day nine hundred ninety-three.

994.title: Sant Attar Singh
994.hook: a holy man of Mastuana who founded schools
994.howItsDone: Sant Attar Singh is remembered at Mastuana, where the gurdwara and the educational institutions linked to his name continue; his followers keep his anniversaries with kirtan and remember him as a sant who joined devotion and education.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jail Letters, and your line was kirtan in prison. Did a steady song carry you through something heavy? Today closes a week that began on the railway at Panja Sahib. Day nine hundred ninety-four.

Crowds come to hear him sing kirtan. He's known for long hours of meditation, and people call him a sant. So when something is built at Mastuana, in the Punjab countryside, beside his name, you might expect a gurdwara with a gold dome and marble floors. There is a gurdwara. But there is also a school, and then a college. Classrooms, teachers, books, and children learning Gurmukhi beside arithmetic. Today: Sant Attar Singh.
screen: `CROWDS FOR KIRTAN.` → `NOT ONLY A GURDWARA.` → `A SCHOOL AT MASTUANA.`

segments.voice: First, the sant. Attar Singh served as a soldier as a young man, and then left that life for one of devotion. He became known across Punjab as a sant, a holy man, who spent long hours in meditation and kirtan and traveled to preach the Gurus' teaching. Tradition says that people took amrit, the Khalsa initiation, after hearing him. Second, the turn. His followers remember him wanting faith and learning to grow together. At Mastuana he founded a school and a college, the Akal College, where Gurmukhi and the Gurus' teaching were taught alongside ordinary subjects. That's today's line: schools, not only temples. Third, the reach. Tradition says he was invited to lay a foundation stone for Banaras Hindu University, a sign of how widely he was respected beyond the Sikh community. He supported education conferences in Punjab, too. Fourth, the root. In the Japji, at Ang 2 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that within the mind are gems, jewels and rubies, if a person listens to the Guru's teaching even once. Some readers hear his schools in that line: there are jewels in a child's mind, and a school is one way to help them be found. And that closes this week: Panja Sahib's train, Jaito's long campaign, the Gurdwara Act, Master Tara Singh, the Rehat Maryada, Jail Letters, written in his cell, and now a sant who built classrooms. Reform, it turns out, needed both courage and chalk.

segments.voice: Two minutes for a classroom. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind a school you know: your own old one, your children's, a school down the street, a Punjabi or Sunday school at a gurdwara or church. Picture a single classroom in it, early in the morning, before anyone arrives. The chairs, the board, the smell of paper. Breathe in, and picture the children coming in. Breathe out, and wish them good teachers and open minds. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Attar Singh, the holy man of Mastuana, a former soldier known for meditation and kirtan, who founded schools and a college so that learning grew beside faith. Today's word.
Your line: schools, not only temples. Today, support a school: donate supplies, help with homework, or offer an hour to a school near you. Day nine hundred ninety-four.
